opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What I found really interesting was that BLOOM gave us a chance to look at the whole picture instead of just one number. Most papers that report a carbon footprint, if they report one at all, only count the energy used to train the final model. With BLOOM, because it was an open, collaborative project through BigScience, we could also look at things people usually leave out.

For example, there's the embodied emissions, meaning the carbon cost of manufacturing the GPUs and servers. There's also the idle consumption of the infrastructure, since a cluster draws power even when it isn't actively computing, and the networking and cooling around it. When we added those up, the total was roughly double what you'd get from counting only the dynamic power of the final training run. That says a lot about how much we've been underestimating.

The second thing was the location. BLOOM was trained on the Jean Zay supercomputer in France, where the grid is mostly nuclear, so the carbon intensity is very low. A model of similar size trained on a coal-heavy grid could have emitted many times more. So where you train matters enormously, maybe more than people expect.

And the third piece, which I think is the most overlooked, is deployment. We ran BLOOM behind an API for a few weeks and measured its energy use while it was serving requests. Even with low traffic, there's a constant baseline cost just from keeping the model loaded on GPUs and ready to respond. If you scale that up to millions of users, inference can quickly overtake training as the main source of emissions.

So for me the takeaway was that a carbon footprint isn't one number. It's a whole life cycle, and we need much more transparency and standardized reporting across the field to understand it properly.

r001.rationale: The response describes measuring several footprint components, but it does not say that detailed training logs enabled the study or that they were used to examine individual development stages.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that surprised me the most was how much of the footprint has nothing to do with training itself. When people talk about the carbon footprint of a model, they tend to think about the GPUs running for however many weeks, and that's it. But when we actually sat down to do a proper life cycle analysis for BLOOM, we found that the dynamic power consumption, the actual compute, was really only about half the story.

So we tried to account for the embodied emissions, meaning the carbon that went into manufacturing the hardware in the first place, the GPUs, the servers, all of that, amortized over their expected lifetime. And then there's the idle power, the energy that the rest of the infrastructure is consuming just to keep the cluster up, the cooling, the networking, the overhead of the data center. And those two things together roughly doubled the number. We ended up at something like 50 tons of CO2 equivalent total, where if you'd only counted the training compute you'd have said around 25.

The other interesting piece was the role of where you train. BLOOM was trained on Jean Zay, which is a supercomputer in France, and the French grid is mostly nuclear, so it's very low carbon. If you'd trained the exact same model on a grid that's heavy on coal or natural gas, the number could have been many times higher. So the location decision ends up mattering as much as, or more than, a lot of the architectural choices people spend their time optimizing.

And then I think the piece that's stuck with me the most, and that I keep coming back to in later work, is deployment. We measured the emissions of BLOOM actually serving requests after training, and it's small per query, but it's constant, it never stops. Training is a one time cost. Inference is forever. And nobody really tracks that, so the field has this habit of putting a big number on training and then kind of ignoring the long tail.

But honestly, the meta lesson for me was just how hard this is to do at all. We could do it for BLOOM because it was an open project and we had access to everything, the hardware specs, the logs, the people who ran the cluster. For most of the models that get released, none of that is available. So part of why we did it was to say, look, here's what it takes to actually do this properly, and here's a template other people could follow if they wanted to be transparent about it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions access to logs as one reason the BLOOM analysis was possible, but it does not say that detailed training logs enabled measuring the footprint of individual development stages.

astra-6.text:
What I found interesting was how much the answer depends on where you draw the boundaries. You can look at the electricity used during the final training run, but that’s only one part of the picture. There’s also the manufacturing of the hardware, the energy the infrastructure consumes even when it isn’t actively training, and all the experimentation that leads up to that final run.

With BLOOM, we had an opportunity to look beyond that single training number and ask what a more complete accounting would look like. And then there’s deployment: training happens once, but people can keep using the model. So the footprint isn’t just a fixed cost you can calculate at the end of training—it also depends on how and where the model is used.

sol-6.1.text:
What was interesting about BLOOM was that we could look beyond the energy used for the final training run. We could also consider the emissions associated with manufacturing the hardware and the electricity consumed by the infrastructure when it wasn’t actively training the model. Those things are often left out of estimates, but they’re part of the footprint too.

It also highlighted how much location matters. The same computation can have a very different carbon footprint depending on the electricity grid powering it. So there isn’t a single number that tells you everything about a model’s environmental impact—you need to understand what’s included and where the work happened.
